newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan govt confirms fall of eastern province.
newsitem.headline: Afghan govt confirms fall of eastern province.

text.p: The Afghan government on Friday confirmed the fall of the eastern province of Laghman to the rebel Taleban Islamic militia, which said it had seized the adjoining Kunar province as well.
There were conflicting reports about the situation in Kunar, which borders Pakistan.

A Taleban source in the northwestern Pakistani town of Peshawar said the province had come under the control of the militia, which has pushed east in the past week to take greater control over strategic provinces.
But other Afghan sources in Pakistan denied this report and said peace negotiations were going on between the Taleban and the pro-government Kunar administration.

However, these sources said the Taleban forces could have captured parts of Kunar in a three-pronged drive they began on Thursday from the newly captured Nangarhar province towards Kunar, Laghman and the strategic town of Sarobi east of capital Kabul.
Afghan government officials in Kabul said Taleban had taken Laghman after government troops pulled back to establish defensive belts in a main plateau overlooking Sarobi, 60 km (40 miles) from Kabul.
Two jets bombed the Sarobi area apparently aiming to hit military targets, which they missed, the officials said.
Amrullah, a spokesman for President Burhanuddin Rabbani's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, accused Pakistan of sending the jets.

He said these jets spent a long time manoeuvering over Sarobi and could not have taken off from Jalalabad, which the Taleban captured on Wednesday, or have come from far away Taleban bases in the southern province of Kandahar and the western province of Herat.
No comment on the charge was immediately available from Pakistan, whom Kabul accuses of helping the Taleban. Islamabad denies the charge.

Taleban, which already controls about half of Afghanistan, including key land routes, is trying to topple President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government and enforce a strict Islamic order throughout the war-shattered country.

Taleban sources in Peshawar also said the militia forces had taken a government post and Torghar mountain in their advance to the strategic town of Sarobi east of Kabul. The rebels were only about 30 km (18 km) from Sarobi late on Friday, they said.
Taleban forces were facing strong resistance from government troops positioned on hills, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said. There was heavy fighting in the area.
Estimates of the size of the militia or number of casualties from Taleban's recent advances were unavailable.
Taleban sources earlier said the militia forces had taken Mehtar Lam before dawn. They later took control of mountainous Alising and the Alingar valley north of it.

Laghman had been controlled by the party of Afghan Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, who joined Rabbani's government in June after agreeing to a peace pact. Kunar had been controlled by a fundamentalist Islamic group called Salfis.
Afghan sources in Pakistan said that the latest Taleban advance was part of the militia's plans to capture maximum territory ahead of any internationally-brokered peace deal.
United Nations Under-Secretary for Political Affairs Marrack Goulding and special peace envoy Norbert Holl arrived in Kabul on Thursday for talks with Afghan leaders.
Rabbani, in a speech in Kabul on Thursday, vowed to fight on and called Taleban "enemies of Afghanistan."
